records.greek: Μὴ ταρασσέσθω ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία· πιστεύετε εἰς τὸν θεόν, καὶ εἰς ἐμὲ πιστεύετε.
records.gloss: Not let be troubled of you the heart; believe in the God, and in me believe.

L.1: "Do not let your heart be troubled; believe in God, and believe in Me also.

R.1: "Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God. Believe in Me too.

decisions.choice: be troubled: shaken, stirred up with fear and distress
decisions.reason: The same verb was used of Jesus himself at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), when he spoke of his coming hour (12:27), and when he announced the betrayal (13:21). He has just told the disciples that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him (13:21-38). Now he tells them not to be shaken by it. He says the same again in 14:27.

decisions.choice: your heart: one heart for the whole group
alternatives: each person's heart, considered one by one
decisions.reason: "Your" is plural and "heart" is singular. The heart is the inner person, where fear and trust live. The singular speaks of the disciples together, as one group facing the same loss; it means the heart of each of them.

decisions.choice: believe ... believe: both are commands
alternatives: You believe in God; believe also in me
You believe in God, and you believe in me
Believe in God, and you believe in me
decisions.reason: The Greek form of the verb is the same for "you believe" and "believe!", so either could be a statement or a command. Reading both as commands fits the command just before ("let your heart not be troubled") and the later call to believe in 14:11. Another common reading takes the first as a statement and the second as a command: "You believe in God; believe also in me." The two clauses stand in a mirror pattern (believe in God / in me believe), which puts trust in Jesus beside trust in God. Either way the point is the same: the cure for a troubled heart is trust in God and in Jesus together.

decisions.choice: Do not let your heart be troubled (L); Do not let your hearts be troubled (B, R)
alternatives: Let not your heart be troubled
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the singular "heart"; Balanced and Readable say "hearts", since English uses the plural when several people are meant (meaning decision m2). The same Greek words return in 14:27, and every level gives them the same English there, so the reader sees Jesus close the thought where he began it.

records.heading: The way to the Father

records.greek: ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ τοῦ πατρός μου μοναὶ πολλαί εἰσιν· εἰ δὲ μή, εἶπον ἂν ὑμῖν ὅτι πορεύομαι ἑτοιμάσαι τόπον ὑμῖν·
records.gloss: In the house of the Father of me dwelling places many are; if but not, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you;

L.2: In the house of My Father there are many dwelling places; but if not, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.

R.2: There are many places to live in My Father's house. If that were not true, I would have told you. In fact, I am going there to get a place ready for you.

decisions.choice: my Father's house: the Father's own home, where he is present
decisions.reason: In 2:16 "my Father's house" was the temple in Jerusalem, but Jesus is now speaking of where he is going: to the Father (13:1, 3; 14:12). The picture is of a large family house with room for many. It speaks of being with the Father, as the next verse says ("so that where I am, you also may be").

decisions.choice: dwelling places: places to stay and live, lasting homes
decisions.reason: The noun comes from the verb "remain" (or "stay"), which John uses often (1:38-39; 15:4-10). It means a place where one stays, not a place one passes through. In 14:23 the same noun returns: the Father and the Son will come and make their dwelling with the one who loves Jesus. So the hope of being with the Father later is matched by his presence now.

decisions.choice: a statement: If it were not so, I would have told you, for I am going to prepare a place for you
alternatives: If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going to prepare a place for you?
If it were not so, I would have told you that I go to prepare a place for you
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates this as a statement, and that is followed here. The linking word is then read as "for": Jesus would have warned them if there were no room, and his going to prepare a place shows that there is. Other editions put a question mark at the end and read the linking word as "that": "If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going to prepare a place for you?" The point is the same either way: Jesus has not misled them.

decisions.choice: the linking word (for / that) is read
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts have the small linking word before "I go"; many later manuscripts lack it, giving "If it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you." The SBLGNT includes it. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: dwelling places (L, B); places to live (R)
decisions.reason: The older English "mansions" once meant simply "places to stay" but now suggests large, grand houses, which the Greek word does not mean (meaning decision m2). "Rooms" is also possible but loses the sense of a lasting home.

decisions.choice: Otherwise (B); If that were not true (R); In fact, I am going there to get a place ready (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "if not" in one natural word. Readable breaks the sentence and shows the link with "In fact": his going to prepare a place is the proof that there is room (meaning decision m3). "There" is supplied: the place is in the Father's house.

records.greek: καὶ ἐὰν πορευθῶ καὶ ἑτοιμάσω τόπον ὑμῖν, πάλιν ἔρχομαι καὶ παραλήμψομαι ὑμᾶς πρὸς ἐμαυτόν, ἵνα ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἦτε.
records.gloss: And if I go and prepare a place for you, again I come and will take along you to myself, so that where am I also you may be.

L.3: And if I go and prepare a place for you, I am coming again, and I will take you to Myself, so that where I am, you also may be.

R.3: After I go and get a place ready for you, I will come back. I will take you to be with Me, so that you will be where I am.

decisions.choice: if I go: a condition that is sure to be met
alternatives: a real doubt whether he will go
decisions.reason: Jesus has said that he is going (13:33, 36; 14:2). The "if" does not raise a doubt about it; it sets out what will follow once it has happened, much like "when".

decisions.choice: I am coming again: his return to bring them to be with him
alternatives: his coming to the disciples after the resurrection only
his coming through the Spirit only
his coming for each believer at death
decisions.reason: The present tense speaks of a sure future. Taking the disciples to himself, so that they will be where he is, points most naturally to his coming at the end, when he brings his people to be with him (compare 21:22-23; 17:24). This same chapter also speaks of other comings: after the resurrection (14:18-19) and in the presence of the Father and the Son with those who love him (14:23). John may intend these to be heard together; the words here do not settle when.

decisions.choice: take you to myself: take you along to be with me
decisions.reason: The verb means to take someone along with oneself, to receive someone into one's company. The stress falls on being with Jesus, which the purpose clause spells out.

decisions.choice: where I am, you also may be: an answer to 13:33, 36
decisions.reason: Jesus told the disciples that they could not come where he was going, not now, but later (13:33, 36). Here he says how "later" will happen. He prays for the same in 17:24, and he said it of anyone who serves him in 12:26.

decisions.choice: when I have gone (B); After I go (R); I will come back and take you to be with me (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "when" or "after" because the condition is certain (meaning decision m1). "Come back" gives the sense of "again", and "to be with me" says plainly what "to myself" means (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: καὶ ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω οἴδατε τὴν ὁδόν.
records.gloss: And where I go you know the way.

L.4: And where I am going, you know the way."

R.4: You know the way to where I am going."

decisions.choice: the shorter text: where I am going, you know the way
alternatives: And where I am going you know, and the way you know
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read a longer sentence: "And where I go you know, and the way you know." The shorter text is found in the oldest manuscripts and is the reading of the SBLGNT. The longer one seems to smooth out the short, compressed sentence. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the way: the road that leads to where Jesus is going
decisions.reason: Jesus uses an ordinary word for a road or path, and Thomas takes it that way (verse 5). Verse 6 shows what Jesus means: he himself is the way to the Father, and the disciples already know him.

decisions.choice: you know the way that leads to where I am going (B); You know the way to where I am going (R)
alternatives: Where I am going, you know the way
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "where I am going" first. Balanced and Readable put "you know the way" first and join the two parts with "that leads to" or "to", which is how English says it.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ Θωμᾶς· Κύριε, οὐκ οἴδαμεν ποῦ ὑπάγεις· πῶς δυνάμεθα τὴν ὁδὸν εἰδέναι;
records.gloss: Says to him Thomas, "Lord, not we know where you go; how are we able the way to know?"

L.5: Thomas says to Him, "Lord, we do not know where You are going; how are we able to know the way?"

R.5: Thomas said, "Lord, we do not know where You are going. Then how can we know the way to get there?"

decisions.choice: Lord: a disciple's address to his master
decisions.reason: Thomas is one of the disciples who follow Jesus (11:16), so the word is "Lord", as with Peter in 13:36-37 and Philip in verse 8.

decisions.choice: Thomas takes "the way" as a road to a place
decisions.reason: Like Peter in 13:36-37, Thomas thinks of a place one could travel to. He does not know where Jesus is going, so he cannot see how they could know the road. His honest question opens the way for Jesus's answer in verse 6. Thomas speaks his doubts plainly elsewhere too (11:16; 20:24-25).

decisions.choice: how can we know the way
alternatives: how do we know the way?
decisions.reason: Some important early manuscripts have a shorter question: "how do we know the way?" The SBLGNT reads "how are we able to know the way?" The meaning is the same. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: says (L); said (B, R); also verses 6, 8 and 9
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told. This applies to every such verb in the passage ("says" in verses 5, 6, 8 and 9).

decisions.choice: Then how can we know the way to get there?
decisions.reason: Readable adds "Then" and "to get there" to show how Thomas's second sentence follows from the first: without knowing the place, he cannot know the road to it.

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή· οὐδεὶς ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸν πατέρα εἰ μὴ δι’ ἐμοῦ.
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "I am the way and the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me.

L.6: Jesus says to him, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.

R.6: Jesus answered him, "I am the way, and I am the truth and the life. The only way anyone can come to the Father is through Me.

decisions.choice: I am the way: one of Jesus's sayings that begin "I am" with a picture
decisions.reason: Here "I am" has a predicate, like "I am the bread of life" (6:35), "I am the light of the world" (8:12), "I am the good shepherd" (10:11) and "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25). The sentence is ordinary in form, but the "I" is stressed: Jesus does not show the way as a guide does; he is the way. He answers Thomas's question about the road with himself.

decisions.choice: the way, and the truth, and the life: the way comes first, and the other two say why he is the way
alternatives: three equal titles with no order among them
a single idea: the true and living way
decisions.reason: Thomas asked about the way, and the next clause explains only the way ("no one comes to the Father except through me"), so "the way" is the main point. "Truth" and "life" say what makes Jesus the way: in him the truth about God is made known (1:14, 17-18; 8:32; 18:37), and in him is the life that comes from God (1:4; 5:26; 11:25). The three are still three nouns joined by "and", each with its article, so each is said of Jesus in its own right.

decisions.choice: No one comes to the Father except through me: Jesus is the only access to the Father
decisions.reason: "Comes to the Father" means coming to God himself, to know him and be with him, which is where Jesus is going (verses 2-4, 12). Only the Son, who has seen the Father, can make him known (1:18; 6:46); compare "I am the door" (10:9). The next verse ties coming to the Father with knowing Jesus.

decisions.choice: I am the way, the truth, and the life (B); I am the way, and I am the truth and the life (R); Only through me does anyone come to the Father (B); The only way anyone can come to the Father is through me (R)
alternatives: I am the way and the truth and the life (B)
No one comes to the Father except through me (B, R)
decisions.reason: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" is the plain English of the Greek; there is no other natural way to say it, and it is the form readers know. The second sentence is put in our own words at Balanced and Readable, which both put "through me" in the place of stress; "answered" is a past tense for the historic present (14:5 r-en-1). Readable repeats "I am" to set the way first (meaning decision m2) and states the second sentence positively. Literal keeps each "and".

records.greek: εἰ ἐγνώκειτέ με, καὶ τὸν πατέρα μου ἂν ᾔδειτε· ἀπ’ ἄρτι γινώσκετε αὐτὸν καὶ ἑωράκατε αὐτόν.
records.gloss: If you had known me, also the Father of me you would have known; from now you know him and have seen him.

L.7: If you had known Me, you would have known My Father also; from now on you know Him and have seen Him."

R.7: If you had truly known Me, you would have known My Father too. But from now on you do know Him. You have seen Him."

decisions.choice: If you had known me, you would have known my Father also
alternatives: If you have come to know me, you will know my Father also
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads a condition contrary to fact, which gently rebukes the disciples: they have not yet truly known Jesus. Some early manuscripts, including one of the oldest papyri and Codex Sinaiticus, read a promise instead: "If you have come to know me, you will know my Father also." Both readings are old, and the promise fits the encouragement of the rest of the verse. The SBLGNT reading is followed. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: they have not yet fully known him
decisions.reason: The form says that they had not known Jesus as he truly is, and so had not known the Father in him. This does not deny that they know him at all (verse 4: "you know the way"). Two different verbs for "know" are used in the two halves; here they mean the same.

decisions.choice: from now on: from this hour of Jesus's going to the Father
alternatives: from the time they first met Jesus
decisions.reason: The hour of his glory has come (13:31-32). From now on the disciples know the Father and have seen him, because they have seen Jesus, as verse 9 explains (compare 1:18; 12:45). "Have seen" is a perfect: they have seen, and it stays true.

decisions.choice: truly known; But from now on you do know him
decisions.reason: Readable adds "truly" to show that the rebuke is about knowing Jesus fully, not about knowing him at all (meaning decision m2), and "But" to show the turn from rebuke to promise.

records.greek: Λέγει αὐτῷ Φίλιππος· Κύριε, δεῖξον ἡμῖν τὸν πατέρα, καὶ ἀρκεῖ ἡμῖν.
records.gloss: Says to him Philip, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."

L.8: Philip says to Him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."

R.8: Philip said to Him, "Lord, let us see the Father. That is all we ask."

decisions.choice: Lord: a disciple's address
decisions.reason: Philip was among the first disciples (1:43-46), so the word is "Lord", as with Thomas in verse 5.

decisions.choice: show us the Father: a request to see God
decisions.reason: Philip asks to see the Father with his eyes. The request recalls Moses asking God, "Show me your glory" (Exodus 33:18), and God answering that no one can see his face and live (Exodus 33:20). John has already said that no one has ever seen God, but the Son has made him known (1:18). Jesus's answer in verse 9 turns on this.

decisions.choice: it is enough for us: we will be satisfied and ask nothing more
decisions.reason: The verb means "to be sufficient". Philip means that one sight of the Father would settle every question.

decisions.choice: we will need nothing more (B); let us see the Father. That is all we ask (R)
alternatives: and it is enough for us
and that will be enough for us
decisions.reason: "It is enough for us" is said in natural English. Readable says "let us see" to make plain that Philip asks for a sight of God (meaning decision m2).

records.heading: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Τοσούτῳ χρόνῳ μεθ’ ὑμῶν εἰμι καὶ οὐκ ἔγνωκάς με, Φίλιππε;
records.gloss: Says to him the Jesus, "So long a time with you I am and not you have known me, Philip?

L.9: Jesus says to him, "So long a time I have been with you, and you have not known Me, Philip?

R.9: Jesus answered, "Philip, I have been with all of you for such a long time. Do you still not know who I am?

decisions.choice: so long a time I am with you: a state that began in the past and still goes on
decisions.reason: The Greek uses the present "I am" with a phrase of time for something that has been true for a long time and is still true. Jesus has been with the disciples since the beginning (1:35-51).

decisions.choice: with you (all) ... you (Philip) have not known me
decisions.reason: "With you" is plural: Jesus has been with all the disciples. "You have not known" is singular and is spoken to Philip by name. Philip's question stands for the whole group, as the plural "you" in verses 7 and 10-11 shows.

decisions.choice: known me: known who I truly am
decisions.reason: Philip knows Jesus as a person, but has not grasped who he is: the one in whom the Father is seen (verse 9b; verse 7). The perfect tense means "have come to know and now know".

decisions.choice: I have been with you all this time (B); I have been with all of you for such a long time (R); Do you still not know who I am? (R)
alternatives: So long a time I am with you
Have I been with you so long
decisions.reason: English uses "have been" for the Greek present with a phrase of time (meaning decision m1). Readable says "all of you" for the plural and adds "who I am" to show what kind of knowing is meant (meaning decision m3); "answered" is a past tense for the historic present (14:5 r-en-1).

records.greek: ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακεν τὸν πατέρα· πῶς σὺ λέγεις· Δεῖξον ἡμῖν τὸν πατέρα;
records.gloss: The [one] having seen me has seen the Father; how you say, 'Show us the Father'?

L.9: The one who has seen Me has seen the Father. How do you say, 'Show us the Father'?

R.9: If you have seen Me, you have seen the Father. So why are you asking Me to show you the Father?

decisions.choice: whoever has seen me has seen the Father: the Father is seen in the Son
decisions.reason: Jesus said the same in public: "the one who sees me sees the one who sent me" (12:45). The Son, who is close to the Father's heart, has made him known (1:18). This does not mean that the Son and the Father are the same person; verse 10 explains it: the Father is in the Son and does his works through him. So Philip's request has already been answered.

decisions.choice: has seen: a seeing that has happened and still counts
decisions.reason: Both verbs are perfects. Whoever has seen Jesus has really seen, and goes on having seen, the Father.

decisions.choice: how can you say: surprise and gentle rebuke
decisions.reason: The "you" is stressed: after all this time, Philip of all people. The question does not ask for an answer; it shows that the request is out of place.

decisions.choice: To have seen me is to have seen the Father (B); If you have seen me, you have seen the Father (R); why are you asking me to show you the Father? (R)
alternatives: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father
How can you say, 'Show us the Father'?
decisions.reason: "The one who has seen" means anyone at all; Balanced and Readable say it in forms that need no pronoun. Readable turns the quoted request into ordinary speech.

records.greek: οὐ πιστεύεις ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί ἐστιν;
records.gloss: Not you believe that I in the Father and the Father in me is?

L.10: Do you not believe that I [am] in the Father and the Father is in Me?

R.10: Philip, surely you believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me?

decisions.choice: Do you not believe ...?: a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: "You" is still singular, spoken to Philip. The form of the question expects agreement: Philip does believe this, at least in part, and should see what follows from it.

decisions.choice: I am in the Father and the Father is in me: the closest unity, while each stays distinct
decisions.reason: Jesus said this to the crowd in Jerusalem (10:38), and he will pray that his followers may share in it (17:21-23). The Father and the Son are two, since one is in the other, yet so close that to see the Son is to see the Father (verse 9). The next sentence shows how this is seen: in Jesus's words and works.

decisions.choice: Philip, surely you believe ...?
decisions.reason: Readable names Philip because the English "you" does not show that Jesus is still speaking to him alone, and "surely" shows that the question expects "yes" (meaning decision m1); the plural "you" returns in the next sentence.

records.greek: τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἐγὼ λέγω ὑμῖν ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐ λαλῶ, ὁ δὲ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοὶ μένων ποιεῖ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: The words that I say to you from myself not I speak, the but Father in me remaining does the works of him.

L.10: The words that I say to you I do not speak from Myself, but the Father who remains in Me does His works.

R.10: The things I tell you do not come from Me on My own. The Father remains in Me, and He is the one who does His works.

decisions.choice: from myself: on my own initiative and authority
decisions.reason: Jesus says again and again that he does and says nothing on his own (5:19, 30; 7:16-18; 8:28; 12:49-50). His words come from the Father who sent him. Two verbs for "say" and "speak" are used; here they mean the same.

decisions.choice: words ... works: Jesus's words are among the Father's works
alternatives: two separate statements, one about words and one about works
decisions.reason: One would expect "the Father speaks the words", but the sentence moves from words to works. Jesus's words and his deeds are one work of the Father, done through him. This leads into verse 11: believe because of the works.

decisions.choice: remains: stays and lives in me
decisions.reason: The verb is the one John uses for lasting union (6:56; 15:4-10), and it is the verb behind the "dwelling places" of verse 2. The Father does not visit Jesus from time to time; he remains in him.

decisions.choice: on my own authority (B); do not come from me on my own (R); remains (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "on my own authority" as in 12:49 (meaning decision m1). "Remains" is the book-wide word for this verb in its theological sense, kept at every level so the link with 15:4-10 can be seen (meaning decision m3). Readable makes the Father the subject of a new sentence.

records.greek: πιστεύετέ μοι ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί· εἰ δὲ μή, διὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτὰ πιστεύετε.
records.gloss: Believe me that I [am] in the Father and the Father in me; if but not, because of the works themselves believe.

L.11: Believe Me that I [am] in the Father and the Father in Me; but if not, believe because of the works themselves.

R.11: All of you, believe Me: I am in the Father, and the Father is in Me. If you cannot believe Me, then believe because of the works themselves, the things you have seen Me do.

decisions.choice: Believe me ... believe: commands to all the disciples
decisions.reason: The verb is now plural: Jesus turns from Philip to the whole group. Both verbs are commands. "Believe me" means to trust what Jesus says, on his word.

decisions.choice: if not: if you will not believe on my word alone
decisions.reason: The words left out are easy to supply from what comes before: if they do not believe what he says, they can believe because of what he does.

decisions.choice: the works themselves: the signs and deeds the Father does through Jesus
decisions.reason: In John, Jesus's "works" are all he does at the Father's bidding, including the signs (5:36; 9:3-4; 10:25, 32, 37-38). They bear witness to who he is. Jesus said the same to his opponents in 10:37-38. Faith that rests on the works is a first step, not the last (compare 20:29).

decisions.choice: Believe me: I am in the Father (B, R); All of you (R); If you cannot believe me (R); the things you have seen me do (R)
alternatives: Believe me that I am in the Father
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable set out what Jesus asks them to believe after a colon. Readable says "All of you" because the English "you" does not show the change from singular to plural (meaning decision m1), spells out "if not" (meaning decision m2), and explains "works" by what the disciples have seen (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ τὰ ἔργα ἃ ἐγὼ ποιῶ κἀκεῖνος ποιήσει, καὶ μείζονα τούτων ποιήσει, ὅτι ἐγὼ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα πορεύομαι·
records.gloss: Truly truly I say to you, the [one] believing in me the works that I do also that one will do, and greater [than] these he will do, because I to the Father am going;

L.12: Truly, truly I say to you, the one who believes in Me, the works that I do, that one also will do; and greater [works] than these they will do, because I am going to the Father.

R.12: I tell you the truth: anyone who believes in Me will do the same works I do. In fact, they will do even greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.

decisions.choice: greater works: greater in reach, done after Jesus has gone to the Father
alternatives: more astonishing miracles than Jesus did
decisions.reason: The reason given is "because I am going to the Father". After his going, Jesus will send the Spirit (7:39; 16:7), and through the disciples' witness the life he gives will reach far beyond the few places and people of his own ministry (4:35-38; 10:16; 17:20; 20:21-23). That seems to be the sense: greater in scope and in what they bring about, not more spectacular miracles. The works are still his, done by the one who believes in him, as verses 13-14 go on to say.

decisions.choice: the one who believes ... that one also: any believer, man or woman
decisions.reason: "The one who believes" means anyone at all who believes in Jesus, not only the apostles in the room. The emphatic "that one also" points back to this believer and puts the stress on the person: the believer too will do what Jesus does.

decisions.choice: because I am going to the Father: Jesus's going makes the greater works possible
decisions.reason: His going away is not a loss for the work but the reason for its growth. He says the same of the Spirit's coming (16:7).

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage.

decisions.choice: greater [works] (L); greater works (B, R); even (R); they / he (L, R)
decisions.reason: "Greater" in the Greek has no noun; "works" is supplied from the first half of the verse. Where English needs a pronoun for the believer, the reader's gender setting gives "they" or "he"; Balanced needs none. Readable adds "In fact" and "even" to mark the step up from "the same works" to "greater works".

records.greek: καὶ ὅ τι ἂν αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου τοῦτο ποιήσω, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ·
records.gloss: And whatever you may ask in the name of me, this I will do, so that may be glorified the Father in the Son;

L.13: And whatever you ask in My name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

R.13: I will do anything you ask for in My name. That way the Father's glory will be shown in the Son.

decisions.choice: in my name: as people who belong to Jesus, by his authority and in keeping with who he is
alternatives: simply saying his name at the end of a prayer
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person. To ask in Jesus's name is to ask as his disciples, joined to him, on the ground of what he is and does, and so for what he would want. It is not a form of words that makes any request certain. This is the first time Jesus speaks of asking in his name; he returns to it in 15:16 and 16:23-26.

decisions.choice: whatever you ask ... I will do it: Jesus himself answers
decisions.reason: The verse does not say whom they ask; verse 14 says "ask me", and 15:16 and 16:23 speak of asking the Father. Here the stress is that Jesus, though going to the Father, will still act for his disciples. This is how the "greater works" of verse 12 will be done.

decisions.choice: so that the Father may be glorified in the Son: the purpose of Jesus's answering
decisions.reason: When Jesus does what his disciples ask, the Father's glory is shown in what the Son does, as it was in his signs (11:4, 40) and will be in his death (13:31-32). Everything leads back to the Father.

decisions.choice: so that in the Son the Father may be glorified (B); That way the Father's glory will be shown in the Son (R)
alternatives: so that the Father may be glorified in the Son
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "in the Son" first, as it put "in him" first in 13:31, to keep the stress on the Son. Readable says that the Father's glory "will be shown", as it did in 13:31, which is what being glorified means here.

records.greek: ἐάν τι αἰτήσητέ με ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου ἐγὼ ποιήσω.
records.gloss: If anything you may ask me in the name of me, I will do.

L.14: If you ask Me anything in My name, I will do [it].

R.14: Yes, ask Me for anything in My name, and I Myself will do it.

decisions.choice: ask me: the word "me" is read
alternatives: If you ask anything in my name, I will do it
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts lack "me", giving "If you ask anything in my name"; this may have been an attempt to fit the verse to 16:23, where the disciples ask the Father. A few manuscripts and early versions lack the whole verse, probably because it seemed to repeat verse 13. The SBLGNT includes the verse with "me", and the oldest manuscripts support it. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: ask me ... I will do it: prayer to Jesus himself, answered by him
decisions.reason: The disciples may ask Jesus himself, and the "I" is stressed: he himself will act. Later he speaks of asking the Father in his name (15:16; 16:23); John holds both together, since the Father and the Son are one in their work (verse 10).

decisions.choice: I myself will do it (B, R); Yes, ask me for anything ..., and (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "I myself" for the stressed "I" (meaning decision m2). Readable begins with "Yes" to show that Jesus is repeating and stressing the promise of verse 13, and turns the condition into an invitation, which in English says the same thing.

records.greek: Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε·
records.gloss: If you love me, the commandments the mine you will keep.

L.15: If you love Me, you will keep My commandments.

R.15: If you love Me, you will obey My commands.

decisions.choice: you will keep (future), as the SBLGNT reads
alternatives: that you may keep my commandments
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads τηρήσετε, a future: "you will keep". Many manuscripts, mostly later ones, have instead the command "keep my commandments", and a few early ones read a form meaning "that you may keep". The forms differ by a letter or two and were easily confused in copying. The future fits the way Jesus goes on in 14:21 and 14:23-24, where keeping his word is what love does. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his commandments
alternatives: obedience as the condition for being loved
decisions.reason: The sentence does not set a price for Jesus's love; it says what love for him looks like. The same link runs through the passage in both directions: whoever keeps his commandments is the one who loves him (14:21), and whoever does not love him does not keep his words (14:24). Compare 1 John 5:3.

decisions.choice: my commandments: all that Jesus has told them, above all the new commandment to love one another
alternatives: the commandments of the Law of Moses
decisions.reason: The Greek stresses that they are his own ("the commandments, the mine"). He has just given the new commandment to love one another as he has loved them (13:34); in 14:23-24 the same thing is called his "word" and his "words". "Keep" means hold on to and obey, as in 8:51.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}, {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}, {{deity_pronoun:we|We}}, {{deity_pronoun:our|Our}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Jesus, for the Father and for the Spirit uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me", "my" and "myself" when Jesus speaks of himself, "you" when Judas speaks to him (14:22), and "we" and "our" when Jesus speaks of the Father and himself (14:23). At the start of a sentence "He" or "My" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: keep ... commandments (L); keep the commandments I have given you (B); obey my commands (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "keep" and "commandments", the words that tie this verse to 13:34 and 14:21. Balanced spells out that these are commandments Jesus himself has given, which is what the stressed "mine" says. Readable uses the plainer "obey" and "commands".

records.heading: The promise of the Advocate

records.greek: κἀγὼ ἐρωτήσω τὸν πατέρα καὶ ἄλλον παράκλητον δώσει ὑμῖν ἵνα ᾖ μεθ’ ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας, ὃ ὁ κόσμος οὐ δύναται λαβεῖν, ὅτι οὐ θεωρεῖ αὐτὸ οὐδὲ γινώσκει· ὑμεῖς γινώσκετε αὐτό, ὅτι παρ’ ὑμῖν μένει καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται.
records.gloss: And I will ask the Father and another Advocate he will give to you, that he may be with you into the age, \v 17 the Spirit of the truth, whom the world not is able to receive, because not it sees him nor knows; you know him, because beside you he remains and in you will be.

L.16: And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate, so that He may be with you forever,
L.17: the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees Him nor knows [Him]; you know Him, because He remains with you and will be in you.

R.16: I will ask the Father for you, and He will give you another Advocate, one like Me. He will be with you forever.
R.17: He is the Spirit of truth. The world, which has turned away from God, cannot receive Him, because it does not see Him or know Him. But you know Him, because He remains with you, and He will be in you.

decisions.choice: another Advocate: a second one of the same kind as Jesus himself
alternatives: an advocate of a different kind
decisions.reason: The word ἄλλον means another of the same sort. Jesus has been with the disciples as their helper, teacher and defender; now that he is going away, the Father will give them another who will do the same for them. 1 John 2:1 uses this same title for Jesus himself, speaking for believers before the Father. And unlike Jesus, who is about to leave them, this one will be with them "forever" (literally "into the age").

decisions.choice: Advocate: one called to stand beside someone and speak for them
decisions.reason: The noun παράκλητον was used of someone called in to stand by a person, especially to speak for them before a court. In John the setting is witness and judgment: the Spirit will testify about Jesus (15:26) and prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment (16:8-11). "Advocate" keeps that setting; "Helper", "Counselor" and "Comforter" each bring out a part of the word's meaning. This is the first of its four occurrences in John (14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7).

decisions.choice: the Spirit of truth: the Holy Spirit, who belongs to the truth and leads Jesus's followers into it
alternatives: a spirit or attitude of truthfulness
decisions.reason: This is God's own Spirit, the Advocate just promised, so it is "the Spirit" and not a human spirit or attitude. He is "of truth" because he comes from the God of truth and makes the truth known: he will guide the disciples into all the truth (16:13) and testify about Jesus, who is the truth (14:6; 15:26).

decisions.choice: the neuter pronouns follow the grammar of the word "Spirit"; they do not make the Spirit a thing
decisions.reason: The word for Spirit, πνεῦμα, is neuter in Greek, so the pronouns that refer back to it are neuter too: ὃ ("which"), αὐτὸ and αὐτό ("it"). This is a rule of agreement, like the gender of nouns in many languages, and says nothing about whether the Spirit is a person. The Advocate does what persons do: he teaches and reminds (14:26), testifies (15:26), convicts, guides, hears and speaks (16:8-13); and in 16:13-14 John uses a masculine pronoun ("that one") for him.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity organized against God
alternatives: all people, without that sense of opposition
decisions.reason: Here "the world" is set against the disciples: it cannot receive the Spirit, because it does not see or know him. This is the world that does not know God and turns against Jesus and his followers (1:10; 15:18-19; 17:14, 25). It cannot receive him, not because the Spirit is hidden, but because of what it is.

decisions.choice: he remains with you and will be in you: the Spirit is present with them now, and will live within them
alternatives: two ways of saying the same thing
decisions.reason: "Remains" is John's key verb μένει, used of the Spirit remaining on Jesus (1:32-33) and of believers remaining in Jesus (15:4-10). "With you" and "in you" are not quite the same: the disciples already know the Spirit, who is at work in Jesus among them, but the Spirit will be given to live within them only after Jesus is glorified (7:39; 20:22). The future "will be" points to that time.

decisions.choice: will be in you (future), as the SBLGNT reads
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ἔσται, "will be". Some early and important manuscripts read the present "is" ("he remains with you and is in you"). The present would make the Spirit's dwelling in the disciples something already true; the future makes it a promise for after Jesus's departure, in line with 7:39 and 16:7. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: whom, {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} for the Spirit; never "it" or "which"
decisions.reason: English pronouns follow the sense, not the grammatical gender of a noun. The Spirit is a person (meaning decision m4), so every level says "he", "him" and "whom", with the deity_pronoun setting as for the Father and the Son. Literal brackets the second "him", which the Greek leaves unstated.

decisions.choice: Advocate, capitalized; forever
decisions.reason: "Advocate" is the book's word for this title at every level (meaning decision m2), capitalized because it names the Spirit. "Into the age" is the Greek idiom for "forever".

decisions.choice: in answer (B); for you, one like {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, which has turned away from God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "in answer" and Readable "for you" to make plain how the two halves of the first clause are linked: the Father gives because the Son asks, and he asks on the disciples' behalf. Readable also explains "another" as "one like me" (meaning decision m1) and says which world is meant (meaning decision m5), since a young reader would take "the world" to mean simply everyone. It keeps the word "world".

records.greek: Οὐκ ἀφήσω ὑμᾶς ὀρφανούς, ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: Not I will leave you orphans, I am coming to you.

L.18: I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you.

R.18: I will not leave you all alone, like children who have no father. I am coming to you.

decisions.choice: orphans: children left without a father, bereft and unprotected
decisions.reason: The word ὀρφανούς means children who have lost a parent, and more widely anyone left without a protector. The picture fits: Jesus has called the disciples "little children" (13:33), and a teacher's disciples could be spoken of as his children. Jesus is about to leave them, but they will not be left without a father's care.

decisions.choice: I am coming to you: above all his return to them after the resurrection, continued in his presence through the Spirit
alternatives: his coming in the Spirit only
his coming at the end of the age (14:3)
decisions.reason: The next verse says that in a little while the world will no longer see him but they will see him (14:19), which points to the risen Jesus coming and standing among them (20:19, 26). But the coming is tied to the promise of the Spirit just before (14:16-17), and in 14:23 the Father and the Son come to make their home with the one who loves Jesus, which is not limited to Easter. In 14:3 "I am coming again" speaks of his final coming. The senses may overlap, and the decision between them is not certain.

decisions.choice: I am coming: present tense of a coming that is certain and near
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the present, as in 14:3, for something about to happen and already as good as begun.

decisions.choice: like orphans with no father (B); all alone, like children who have no father (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the picture of children left without a father (meaning decision m1) and say it plainly, so that it is not heard as a legal term only. Literal says "orphans".

records.greek: ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ ὁ κόσμος με οὐκέτι θεωρεῖ, ὑμεῖς δὲ θεωρεῖτέ με, ὅτι ἐγὼ ζῶ καὶ ὑμεῖς ζήσετε.
records.gloss: Yet a little and the world me no longer sees, but you see me, because I live and you will live.

L.19: Yet a little [while] and the world no longer sees Me, but you see Me; because I live, you also will live.

R.19: Soon the world will not see Me anymore. But you will see Me. Because I am alive, you will have life too.

decisions.choice: a little while, and the world will no longer see me: his death is near, and after it only his disciples will see him
decisions.reason: "Yet a little" means in a short time, as in 13:33 and 16:16-19. The present tenses "sees" speak of what is about to happen. After his death the world will not see Jesus again; the risen Jesus shows himself only to his disciples (20:19-29; 21:1), which is the question Judas raises in 14:22.

decisions.choice: because I live, you also will live: the reason clause goes with what follows it
alternatives: you see me, because I live and you will live
decisions.reason: The word ὅτι can begin a new statement ("because I live, you will live") or give the reason they will see him ("you will see me, because I live and you will live"). The first is the more natural balance of the two short clauses, and it states a theme of the Gospel: the life of believers depends on the life of Jesus (6:57; 11:25-26). Either way, his rising is the ground of their seeing and their living.

decisions.choice: I live ... you will live: Jesus's risen life, which he shares with those who believe
decisions.reason: "I live" is in the present: Jesus has life in himself (5:26), which death cannot hold. "You will live" is the eternal life he gives, which begins now and does not end with death (11:25-26).

decisions.choice: the world: humanity that has rejected Jesus
decisions.reason: As in 14:17, the world here is set against the disciples: those who do not believe in him and will not see him again after his death.

decisions.choice: will see (B, R); I am alive ... you will have life (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the present "sees" into the future, since it speaks of the days after his death (meaning decision m1). Readable says "I am alive" and "you will have life" to make clear that real life, not simply staying alive, is meant.

records.greek: ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ γνώσεσθε ὑμεῖς ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρί μου καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: In that the day will know you that I in the Father of me and you in me and I in you.

L.20: In that day you will know that I [am] in My Father, and you in Me, and I in you.

R.20: When that day comes, you will understand that I am in My Father. You will understand that you are in Me, and that I am in you.

decisions.choice: that day: the time after the resurrection, when they see him again and receive the Spirit
alternatives: the last day, at the end of the age
decisions.reason: In the farewell words "that day" is the time that follows the "little while" of 14:19 and 16:16, when their grief turns to joy and they ask the Father in Jesus's name (16:22-26). It begins when the risen Jesus comes to them and breathes the Spirit on them (20:19-22).

decisions.choice: I in my Father, you in me, I in you: the bond of Father and Son is opened to the disciples
decisions.reason: Jesus has just said that he is in the Father and the Father in him (14:10-11). Now the disciples are drawn into that union: they are in him and he is in them, as the vine and the branches (15:4-5) and as he prays in 17:21-23. What they cannot grasp now they will come to know when it is true of them.

decisions.choice: you will know: come to understand from their own experience
decisions.reason: The verb γνώσεσθε is the ordinary "know"; here it is the knowing that comes when what was promised has happened (compare 8:28; 13:7).

decisions.choice: [am] (L); come to know, am, are, and that (B); you will understand ... and that (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb in the clauses after "that". Literal brackets the first "am" and leaves the rest as the Greek has it; Balanced supplies the verbs and says "come to know" for the knowing of experience (meaning decision m3); Readable breaks the sentence in two and repeats "you will understand" so that each clause is clear. The Literal wording is the only natural way to follow the Greek word for word.

records.greek: ὁ ἔχων τὰς ἐντολάς μου καὶ τηρῶν αὐτὰς ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν ὁ ἀγαπῶν με· ὁ δὲ ἀγαπῶν με ἀγαπηθήσεται ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός μου, κἀγὼ ἀγαπήσω αὐτὸν καὶ ἐμφανίσω αὐτῷ ἐμαυτόν.
records.gloss: The [one] having the commandments of me and keeping them, that one is the [one] loving me; and the [one] loving me will be loved by the Father of me, and I will love him and will show to him myself.

L.21: The one who has My commandments and keeps them, that one is the one who loves Me; and the one who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love them and will show Myself to them."

R.21: Anyone who knows My commands and obeys them is the person who really loves Me. My Father will love everyone who loves Me. I will love them too, and I will show Myself to them."

decisions.choice: has my commandments: has received them and holds them as his own
decisions.reason: To "have" his commandments is to have been given them and to hold on to them; "keeps them" adds that they are carried out. Jesus has given his commandments to these disciples (13:34; 15:10-12).

decisions.choice: that one is the one who loves me: love for Jesus is known by keeping his commandments
decisions.reason: The pronoun ἐκεῖνός ("that one") points back with emphasis: it is this person, and no other, who loves him. The sentence turns 14:15 around: there love leads to keeping, here keeping shows the love.

decisions.choice: will be loved by my Father: the Father's love rests on those who love the Son
alternatives: the Father begins to love them only because they love the Son
decisions.reason: This does not mean the love is earned: God loved the world first (3:16). It means that those who love the Son are taken into the love of the Father and the Son for each other (16:27; 17:23, 26).

decisions.choice: show myself: make himself plainly seen and known
decisions.reason: The verb ἐμφανίσω means to make visible or make known. Jesus will show himself to the one who loves him, not to the world (14:19). The risen Jesus did appear to his disciples (20:19-29), and he will also make himself known through the Spirit (14:23, 26). Judas takes up the same verb in 14:22.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: The one who loves Jesus may be a man or a woman, so the pronouns for that person use the gender setting.

decisions.choice: show myself (all levels); knows my commands (R)
decisions.reason: "Show" is a plain word for this verb, and every level uses it again in 14:22, so that Judas is heard repeating what Jesus has just said. Readable says "knows" for "has" (meaning decision m1) and adds "really" for the emphasis of "that one" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: λέγει αὐτῷ Ἰούδας, οὐχ ὁ Ἰσκαριώτης· Κύριε, τί γέγονεν ὅτι ἡμῖν μέλλεις ἐμφανίζειν σεαυτὸν καὶ οὐχὶ τῷ κόσμῳ;
records.gloss: Says to him Judas, not the Iscariot, "Lord, what has happened that to us you are about to show yourself and not to the world?"

L.22: Judas (not the Iscariot) says to Him, "Lord, what has happened, that You are going to show Yourself to us and not to the world?"

R.22: Another of the disciples named Judas (not Judas Iscariot) asked Him, "Lord, why will You show Yourself only to us? Why not to the world?"

decisions.choice: Judas, not Iscariot: the disciple Luke calls "Judas of James"
decisions.reason: Luke's lists of the Twelve include a second Judas, "Judas of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), which may mean son of James. Mark 3:18 and Matthew 10:3 have Thaddaeus in that place, which suggests the same man was known by two names, though this is not certain. John adds "not Iscariot" because Judas Iscariot has already left the room (13:30).

decisions.choice: what has happened that: how can it be, what has changed, that
decisions.reason: The question asks what has come about to make Jesus act this way. Judas seems to expect that the Messiah will show himself openly to all, as Jesus's brothers once urged him to show himself to the world (7:4).

decisions.choice: the world: people in general, those outside the circle of disciples
decisions.reason: In Judas's mouth "the world" means everyone else, the public; he does not yet see what Jesus has said about the world that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17). Jesus answers by saying to whom he and the Father will come (14:23).

decisions.choice: says (L); said, asked (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense ("says") to make a scene vivid. Literal keeps the present; Balanced and Readable use the past, as stories are normally told, and Readable says "asked" because Judas asks a question. This is the only such verb in the passage.

decisions.choice: not Judas Iscariot (B, R); Another of the disciples named Judas (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the name so that "Iscariot" is clearly a name for the other Judas. Readable says this is another disciple, which the narrative makes clear (meaning decision m1).

records.greek: ἀπεκρίθη Ἰησοῦς καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἐάν τις ἀγαπᾷ με τὸν λόγον μου τηρήσει, καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ἀγαπήσει αὐτόν, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλευσόμεθα καὶ μονὴν παρ’ αὐτῷ ποιησόμεθα.
records.gloss: Answered Jesus and said to him, "If anyone loves me, the word of me he will keep, and the Father of me will love him, and to him we will come and a dwelling place with him we will make."

L.23: Jesus answered and said to him, "If anyone loves Me, they will keep My word, and My Father will love them, and We will come to them and make [a] dwelling place with them.

R.23: Jesus answered, "Anyone who loves Me will obey My teaching. My Father will love them. And My Father and I will come to them and make Our home with them.

decisions.choice: if anyone loves me, he will keep my word: true of every believer, not only the Eleven
decisions.reason: Jesus answers Judas by widening the promise: "anyone" who loves him. The answer does not say why he will not show himself to the world, but to whom he will show himself: to those whose love for him is seen in keeping his word (14:15, 21).

decisions.choice: my word: the whole of Jesus's message
decisions.reason: The singular "word" is his teaching taken as a whole (8:31, 51; 17:6); in 14:24 the plural "words" means the same teaching in its many sayings, and "commandments" in 14:15, 21 says the same thing from another side.

decisions.choice: we will come and make our dwelling with him: the Father and the Son will live with the believer
alternatives: a coming only at the end of the age
decisions.reason: "We" is the Father and the Son together. This is how Jesus will show himself to those who love him and not to the world (14:22): not by a public display but by coming to live with them, through the Spirit who will be in them (14:17).

decisions.choice: dwelling place: the same word as the "dwelling places" in the Father's house (14:2)
decisions.reason: The noun μονὴν is used in the New Testament only here and in 14:2, and comes from the verb "remain". In 14:2 Jesus goes to prepare a place for the disciples among the many dwelling places in his Father's house; here the Father and the Son make their dwelling with the one who loves him. The promise runs both ways, and the shared word keeps the two verses together. It is a lasting home, not a short stay.

decisions.choice: Jesus replied (B); Jesus answered (R)
alternatives: Jesus answered and said to him (Literal)
decisions.reason: "Answered and said" is a common Greek way of introducing a reply; Balanced and Readable use one verb. It is clear who is being answered.

decisions.choice: [a] dwelling place (L); our dwelling place (B); our home (R); my word (L, B); my teaching (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "dwelling place" so that the reader can see the link with "dwelling places" in 14:2 (meaning decision m4). Readable says "home", the plain word, and names "my Father and I" for "we" (meaning decision m3); it says "teaching" for "word" (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: {{gender:they|he}}, {{gender:them|him}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" may be a man or a woman, so the pronouns for that person use the gender setting. "Him" in "said to him" is Judas and takes no span.

records.greek: ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν με τοὺς λόγους μου οὐ τηρεῖ· καὶ ὁ λόγος ὃν ἀκούετε οὐκ ἔστιν ἐμὸς ἀλλὰ τοῦ πέμψαντός με πατρός.
records.gloss: The [one] not loving me the words of me not keeps; and the word which you hear not is mine but of the having sent me Father.

L.24: The one who does not love Me does not keep My words; and the word that you hear is not Mine but [is] of the Father who sent Me.

R.24: Anyone who does not love Me does not obey My teaching. And the message you are hearing does not come from Me. It comes from the Father, who sent Me.

decisions.choice: whoever does not love me does not keep my words: the other side of 14:23
decisions.reason: Jesus states the reverse of what he has just said. It also answers Judas: the world does not love him and does not keep his word, and so the Father and the Son do not come to make their home with it.

decisions.choice: my words ... the word: Jesus's teaching, first as many sayings, then as one message
decisions.reason: The plural "words" and the singular "word" refer to the same teaching (compare 14:23). John moves between the two without a change of sense, as in 12:47-48.

decisions.choice: not mine but the Father's: the message comes from the Father, who sent Jesus
alternatives: Jesus disowns the words as not his own
decisions.reason: Jesus does not deny that he speaks these words. He says where they come from: he speaks only what the Father who sent him has given him to say (7:16; 8:28; 12:49-50; 14:10). So to reject his word is to reject the Father's.

decisions.choice: it belongs to the Father (B); does not come from me. It comes from the Father (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "not mine but of the Father". Balanced says the word belongs to the Father; Readable says where the message comes from, which is what being the Father's word means here (meaning decision m3). Readable says "teaching" and "message" for "words" and "word", as in 14:23.

records.greek: Ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν παρ’ ὑμῖν μένων·
records.gloss: These things I have spoken to you beside you remaining.

L.25: These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you.

R.25: I have told you these things while I am still here with you.

decisions.choice: remaining with you: staying in their company, still present with them
alternatives: remaining in the theological sense of a lasting union (15:4-10)
decisions.reason: Here the verb has its ordinary sense: Jesus is still with them, but not for long (13:33; 14:28). The same words, "remains with you", were just used of the Spirit (14:17). The Spirit will stay with the disciples as Jesus is about to stop doing in the same way, which leads into verse 26.

decisions.choice: these things I have spoken: the teaching he has given them up to now, especially this evening
decisions.reason: "These things" looks back over what he has said (also 15:11; 16:1, 4, 25, 33). It sets what Jesus has said while present against what the Spirit will teach and bring back to their minds after he has gone (verse 26).

decisions.choice: while I am still with you (B); still here with you (R)
decisions.reason: "Still" brings out what the participle implies in this setting: his time with them is coming to an end (meaning decision m1). Literal keeps "remaining" so the link with 14:17 can be seen.

records.heading: Peace I leave with you

records.greek: ὁ δὲ παράκλητος, τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ὃ πέμψει ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου, ἐκεῖνος ὑμᾶς διδάξει πάντα καὶ ὑπομνήσει ὑμᾶς πάντα ἃ εἶπον ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: The but advocate, the Spirit the Holy, which will send the Father in the name of me, that one you will teach all things and will remind you all things which I said to you.

L.26: But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, He will teach you all things and will remind you of all things that I said to you.

R.26: But the Father will send the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, in My name. He will teach you everything. He will remind you of everything I have told you.

decisions.choice: the Advocate: one called to stand beside another and speak or act for them
decisions.reason: The word was used of someone who stands by a person, above all in a court, to plead for them. In John the setting is testimony and judgment: the Advocate testifies about Jesus (15:26) and proves the world wrong (16:8-11). He also teaches and reminds (here) and guides (16:13), so the help he gives is wider than the courtroom. 1 John 2:1 uses the same word of Jesus pleading with the Father; 14:16 calls the Spirit "another" Advocate, so Jesus has been one for them already.

decisions.choice: the Holy Spirit: God's own Spirit, the Advocate promised in 14:16-17
decisions.reason: "The Holy Spirit" names the Advocate and shows who he is: the Spirit of God, called "the Spirit of truth" in 14:17. It is the Spirit who came down on Jesus (1:32-33) and whom he will give to those who believe in him (7:39; 20:22).

decisions.choice: a neuter relative pronoun, then a masculine one: grammatical agreement, with the Advocate spoken of as a person
alternatives: the neuter means the Spirit is an impersonal force
the masculine is a deliberate statement that the Spirit is a person
decisions.reason: The word for spirit is neuter, so the pronoun that follows it ("which") is neuter by the rules of Greek grammar, as in 14:17; this says nothing about whether the Spirit is a thing. The resuming word "that one" is masculine, agreeing with "the Advocate" at the head of the sentence, so grammar can explain it too, and it does not prove a point on its own. What shows the Spirit as personal is what he does: he is sent, teaches, reminds, testifies (15:26), hears and speaks (16:13). The masculine word is emphatic: he and no other will teach them.

decisions.choice: in my name: sent on Jesus's behalf, as his representative and in answer to his request
alternatives: sent to make Jesus's name known
decisions.reason: To act in someone's name is to act with their authority and on their behalf (5:43; 10:25). Jesus has said he will ask the Father to send the Advocate (14:16); the Father sends him as Jesus's representative, to carry on what Jesus has begun.

decisions.choice: teach all things and remind of all that Jesus said: two sides of one work, centered on Jesus's own words
alternatives: all things: every kind of knowledge
decisions.reason: "All things" is defined by the second clause: the Spirit's teaching brings back to mind and opens up what Jesus said. John shows this happening: after Jesus was raised, the disciples remembered what he had said and understood it (2:22; 12:16). The Spirit does not bring a different message but makes Jesus's message known (16:13-14).

decisions.choice: the Advocate
decisions.reason: The book uses "the Advocate" at every level, because John's setting is testimony and judgment (meaning decision m1). Other well-known renderings are Helper, Counselor and Comforter; each catches part of the sense.

decisions.choice: whom; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The Spirit is never "it" in this translation. The neuter Greek pronoun is grammatical agreement only (meaning decision m3), so English uses the personal "who", "whom" and "he". "He" takes the deity pronoun setting like every pronoun for God; the relatives "who" and "whom" do not, as nowhere else in the translation does a relative pronoun take it. Balanced turns "he" into "is the one who" to keep the emphasis of the masculine word; Readable starts new sentences with plain "He".

records.greek: εἰρήνην ἀφίημι ὑμῖν, εἰρήνην τὴν ἐμὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν· οὐ καθὼς ὁ κόσμος δίδωσιν ἐγὼ δίδωμι ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: Peace I leave to you, peace the my I give to you; not as the world gives I give to you.

L.27: Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you.

R.27: I am leaving you peace. I am giving you My own peace. I do not give the way the world gives.

decisions.choice: peace: the farewell wish of shalom, given new content as Jesus's own gift
alternatives: peace as the absence of war or conflict
decisions.reason: "Peace" was the ordinary greeting and farewell among Jews, a wish for wholeness and well-being from God. Jesus, about to leave, uses the parting word but does more than wish it: he leaves it and gives it, and it is "my" peace. It is the peace he has with the Father and gives to those who are his, the peace they may have "in me" even in the world's trouble (16:33). The risen Jesus greets them with the same word (20:19, 21, 26). Peace is a key term.

decisions.choice: leave: leave behind as a parting gift, as someone going away leaves something to those who stay
decisions.reason: The verb often means to let go or forgive, but here, with "to you", it means to leave something behind for others. The words are those of one who is departing (14:28).

decisions.choice: not as the world gives: unlike the world's peace, Jesus's gift is real and does not depend on circumstances
alternatives: not in the way the world gives presents
decisions.reason: The contrast is with the world in John's sense, human life apart from God. The world can wish peace, as in a greeting, or offer a peace that lasts only while things go well; it has trouble to give (16:33). Jesus gives what he says, and his peace holds when he is put to death and they are scattered (16:32-33). The "I" is emphatic, setting his giving against the world's.

decisions.choice: Peace I leave with you
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "peace" first in both clauses, and there is no natural way to keep that order other than the familiar wording. Balanced keeps it for the first clause and then stresses "my own peace". Readable uses ordinary word order.

decisions.choice: my own peace
decisions.reason: The Greek has a fuller form of "my", standing after the noun with its own article, which stresses it. "Own" carries that stress.

records.greek: μὴ ταρασσέσθω ὑμῶν ἡ καρδία μηδὲ δειλιάτω.
records.gloss: Not let be troubled of you the heart nor let it be fearful.
pieces: let them give way to fear

L.27: Do not let your heart be troubled, nor let it be fearful.

R.27: Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not be afraid.

decisions.choice: the same command as 14:1, closing the first part of the farewell talk
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats the words he began with in 14:1. The repeat frames what lies between: his going to the Father, his coming back, the Spirit and the peace he leaves give them reason not to be troubled. The word for "troubled" was used of Jesus himself as he faced death (11:33; 12:27; 13:21).

decisions.choice: your heart: one heart for many people, each one's heart
alternatives: the group as a whole, with one shared heart
decisions.reason: "Your" is plural but "heart" is singular, as in 14:1. Greek often speaks so of something each person has one of. The sense is each of them, inwardly.

decisions.choice: be fearful: lose courage, shrink back in fear before danger
alternatives: be cowardly in a shameful sense
decisions.reason: The verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to be timid or lose heart when danger comes. The related noun and adjective are used for cowardice and fearfulness (Matthew 8:26; 2 Timothy 1:7). Jesus is not scolding them; he tells them not to let fear master them as the hour comes (14:30).

decisions.choice: your hearts (B, R); give way to fear (B); do not be afraid (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make "hearts" plural, the natural way to speak of many people's hearts (meaning decision m2). This sentence should read the same as 14:1. Balanced says "give way to fear" for the sense of losing courage; Readable says it simply.

records.greek: ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐγὼ εἶπον ὑμῖν· Ὑπάγω καὶ ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.
records.gloss: You heard that I said to you, "I go away and I come to you."

L.28: You heard that I said to you, 'I am going away, and I am coming to you.'

R.28: You heard Me tell you, 'I am going away, but I will come back to you.'

decisions.choice: I am going away and I am coming: present tenses that look to what is about to happen
decisions.reason: Jesus refers back to what he has said in this talk (14:2-4, 18). Both verbs are present, as is common in Greek of something certain and near: the going has already begun, and the coming is as sure.

decisions.choice: I am coming to you: his return to them after his death, which may include his coming at the end
alternatives: only his coming at the end of the age
only his coming in the Spirit
decisions.reason: In 14:18-19 the coming is soon ("in a little while ... you will see me"), which fits his appearing after the resurrection (20:19-20) and his presence through the Spirit (14:23). In 14:3 he speaks of coming again to take them to himself. The text does not separate these, and the words here can include them all.

decisions.choice: leaving, and I am coming back (B); I will come back (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "leaving" for the plain going away. "Back" makes clear that the one who goes is the one who comes. Readable uses the future for the present tense that points ahead (meaning decision m1) and "but" to show the contrast.

records.greek: εἰ ἠγαπᾶτέ με ἐχάρητε ἄν, ὅτι πορεύομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα, ὅτι ὁ πατὴρ μείζων μού ἐστιν.
records.gloss: If you were loving me, you would have rejoiced, that I go to the Father, because the Father greater than me is.

L.28: If you loved Me, you would have rejoiced that I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.

R.28: If you loved Me, you would be glad that I am going to the Father, because He is greater than I am.

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: their love is not yet glad for him
alternatives: a flat denial that they love him at all
decisions.reason: The form says the condition is not met: if you loved me (as love would), you would have rejoiced. Jesus does not deny that they love him (14:21, 23; 16:27). Their grief looks at their own loss; love that looked at him would be glad that he goes home to the Father.

decisions.choice: the Father is greater: as the one who sent the Son, to whom the Son, having done what he was sent to do, now returns
alternatives: greater than the Son in the humble state he took on earth
decisions.reason: The sentence gives the reason for gladness: Jesus is going to the one who sent him (7:33; 16:5) and will share again the glory he had with him (17:5). Throughout John the Father is the one who sends and commands and the Son the one sent, who does his will (5:19, 30; 8:29; 14:31). The same Gospel says that the Word was God (1:1) and records Jesus saying "I and the Father are one" (10:30), and his claims were heard as making himself equal to God (5:18). This sentence speaks of the Son's relation to the Father in his mission; it does not discuss what the Father and the Son are in their being. The word "greater" has been understood in more than one way.

decisions.choice: because I am going to the Father (SBLGNT)
alternatives: because I said, I am going to the Father (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "I said" before "I am going", repeating the words of the first half of the verse. The earliest manuscripts lack it. The meaning is the same. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Father (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "my Father is greater than I". The earliest manuscripts have "the Father". The sense is not changed. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: would be glad
decisions.reason: In English the past form "would have rejoiced" can sound as if the moment were over; the gladness Jesus means belongs to now, as he goes. "Glad" is the everyday word.

records.greek: καὶ νῦν εἴρηκα ὑμῖν πρὶν γενέσθαι, ἵνα ὅταν γένηται πιστεύσητε.
records.gloss: And now I have told you before to happen, so that whenever it happens you may believe.

L.29: And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe.

R.29: I have told you this now, before it happens. Then, when it happens, you will believe.

decisions.choice: the same purpose as in 13:19: what Jesus foretells will, when it comes true, lead them to believe
decisions.reason: In 13:19 Jesus said the same about Judas's betrayal, adding "that I am". Here "believe" stands without an object: they will believe in him, seeing that what he said came true (2:22). Foretelling what is to come marks the true God in Isaiah (Isaiah 41:22-23; 46:9-10).

decisions.choice: it happens: his going away to the Father through his death, and his coming again
decisions.reason: The unnamed "it" is what he has just spoken of in verse 28: his departure to the Father, which takes place through his arrest and death, and his return to them.

decisions.choice: this
decisions.reason: Readable supplies "this" for what Jesus has told them, which the Greek leaves understood, and splits the sentence.

records.greek: οὐκέτι πολλὰ λαλήσω μεθ’ ὑμῶν, ἔρχεται γὰρ ὁ τοῦ κόσμου ἄρχων· καὶ ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν, ἀλλ’ ἵνα γνῷ ὁ κόσμος ὅτι ἀγαπῶ τὸν πατέρα, καὶ καθὼς ἐνετείλατο μοι ὁ πατὴρ οὕτως ποιῶ.
records.gloss: No longer many things I will speak with you, comes for the of the world ruler; and in me he has not nothing, \v 31 but so that may know the world that I love the Father, and as commanded me the Father, so I do.

L.30: I will no longer speak many things with you, for the ruler of the world is coming, and in Me he has nothing;
L.31: but so that the world may know that I love the Father, and just as the Father commanded Me, so I do.

R.30: I will not talk with you much longer, because Satan, the ruler of the world, is coming. He has no power over Me.
R.31: But I do just what the Father has told Me to do, so that the world will know that I love the Father.

decisions.choice: the ruler of the world: Satan, now coming against Jesus through those who arrest him
decisions.reason: The same title as in 12:31 and 16:11, there with "this world". He is the devil, who has put the betrayal into Judas's heart and entered him (13:2, 27); his coming is the coming of Judas and the arresting party (18:2-3).

decisions.choice: he has nothing in me: he has no claim on Jesus and no hold over him
alternatives: there is nothing in Jesus that belongs to him
he will find nothing in Jesus to accuse
decisions.reason: The phrase, "in me he has nothing", is a way of saying that the devil has no rights over Jesus and no power to take him. Jesus has no sin that would give him a hold (8:46). So Jesus's death is not the devil's victory: Jesus lays down his life of his own accord (10:18). The other readings come to nearly the same thing.

decisions.choice: the purpose clause goes with "so I do": the SBLGNT puts a full stop after "I do"
alternatives: the purpose clause goes with "Rise, let us go from here": so that the world may know that I love the Father and do as he commanded, rise, let us go
decisions.reason: The Greek has no punctuation of its own. With the SBLGNT, the sentence ends at "I do", and "but so that the world may know" leads to what Jesus does: he obeys the Father, and that obedience shows his love. The "and" before "just as" is then loosely attached, as often in John. The text can also be punctuated with a comma at "I do", so that the purpose clause leads into the command to rise and go out, to meet the ruler who is coming. Both give the same picture: Jesus goes to his death to obey the Father.

decisions.choice: Jesus's love for the Father is shown in his doing what the Father commanded, that is, going to the cross
decisions.reason: This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus says in so many words that he loves the Father. He shows it as he asks his disciples to show their love: by keeping commands (14:15, 21). The command is that he lay down his life and take it up again (10:18; 12:49-50). The world, set against God, will see this at the cross (12:32; 17:21, 23).

decisions.choice: Satan, the ruler of the world
decisions.reason: As in 12:31, Readable names Satan, whom the title means (meaning decision m1); Jesus is the one speaking, and he knows who the ruler is. Every level keeps the title as in 12:31; here the Greek has "the world" without "this".

decisions.choice: He has no hold on me (B); no power over me (R); Readable puts the purpose clause last
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means (meaning decision m2). Readable puts what Jesus does first and the reason after, which is easier to follow; the sense is the same.

records.greek: Ἐγείρεσθε, ἄγωμεν ἐντεῦθεν.
records.gloss: Rise, let us go from here.

L.31: Rise, let us go from here.

R.31: Get up. Let us leave this place.

decisions.choice: rise: get up from the table where they have been reclining at the meal
alternatives: rise in the sense of being raised
decisions.reason: At a festive meal people reclined on couches (13:23, 25). The verb means to get up, here from the meal, ready to leave.

decisions.choice: a real call to leave, though the talk goes on and the departure is told only at 18:1
alternatives: they leave now and Jesus goes on speaking on the way
the farewell talks were joined together and this call once led straight to 18:1
the words are a call to go out to meet what is coming, more than a signal to walk out
decisions.reason: The words are plain: Jesus tells them to get up and go. Yet chapters 15 to 17 follow without any mention of moving, and only in 18:1 does John say that Jesus went out with his disciples across the Kidron valley. It may be that they leave now and the talk and prayer of chapters 15 to 17 are spoken on the way. Or the farewell discourses may have been joined together, so that 14:31 once led straight to 18:1. "Let us go" may also be a call to go out and meet the ruler of the world (14:30) in obedience, whenever they moved. The text does not settle which is right.

decisions.choice: Get up; let us go from here (B); Let us leave this place (R)
decisions.reason: "Get up" is the everyday command for rising from a table; "Rise" and "Arise" sound formal. Readable says plainly where they are going: away from the place of the meal.
